🍎 Lesson plan · 🌱 Basics · Lesson 4

Lesson plan: Generative AI & Chatbots

How chatbots and image generators create brand-new content.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • explain that generative AI creates new content, and give examples;
  • describe how a large language model writes: it predicts the next token, again and again;
  • explain what a hallucination is, and use chatbots wisely: check the facts and keep personal data private.

Warm-up

Have you ever asked a chatbot something and got a wrong answer? What happened?

Expect stories of confident mistakes. Keep them for the discussion about hallucinations.

Reading

Students read the lesson “Generative AI & Chatbots”. Students look for what “LLM” and “token” mean, and for why a chatbot can invent facts.

Activity: Mini-lab “Be the language model”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 4: the start of a sentence, “After school, I like to…”, and six possible next words with their chances.
  2. At temperature 1.0 they press “Generate next word” ten times and keep a tally of the words they get.
  3. They move the temperature to the lowest and then to the highest setting, and fill in the worksheet's table.
  4. Pairs explain why a chatbot can give a different answer each time you ask.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers write a sentence start of their own and invent six next words with chances that add up to 100%.

Discussion questions

  • Why does a chatbot sound so sure, even when it is wrong?
  • When is it fine to use a chatbot for schoolwork, and when is it not?
  • What should you never type into a chatbot? Why?
  • Low or high temperature: which would you want for a maths answer, and which for a poem?

Exit ticket

In one sentence, explain what a hallucination is, and give one way to catch one.

Quick check. A chatbot isn't connected to a search tool. Where does its answer about a historical event come from?
Right answer: From patterns in the text it learned from in training

Easier and harder

Easier. Before the mini-lab, play the game on paper: the class suggests next words for “After school, I like to…”, and you tally them on the board as chances.

Harder. Students write two prompts for the same task, one vague and one clear (what you need, some context, the format), and explain which would get the better answer and why.
